newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Cyprus talks fizzling out in Switzerland.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus talks fizzling out in Switzerland.

text.p: Inconclusive unity talks for Cyprus drew to an end in Switzerland on Friday with both sides accusing each other of blocking a deal and retreating to entrenched positions they have held for over 20 years.
Greek and Turkish Cypriot officials agreed that the five-day gathering was a failure and the atmosphere worse than July`s opening round in New York.
"The result is a failure. Even the climate is worse than before," said Nicos Anastasiades, president of the ruling Democratic Rally Party in the Greek Cypriot south.
"Unfortunately, the deadlock is due to the intransigent attitude of (Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf) Denktash and Turkey. Nobody knows how they will manage to bring us back to the table."
Denktash, in turn, has been quick to blame the Greek Cypriot side for the impasse.
U.N. mediator Diego Cordovez rescheduled a Saturday news conference in Geneva to Friday at the venue of the talks here.

Officials said there was no date fixed for a further round and no breakthrough document on the table between president Glafcos Clerides of the internationally recognised Greek Cypriot state, and Denktash.
They said the only question still unanswered was the wording of a possible statement acceptable to both sides which the United Nations, desperate to keep momentum going, was trying to draft.
A European Union decision to start entry talks for Cyprus early next year has brought fresh urgency to efforts to solve the decades-old conflict.

But western diplomats are aware of the risks of pushing for a quick solution which may provoke Denktash into union with Turkey after Ankara said it would move toward partial integration with the north.

Diplomats fear the eastern Mediterranean island, a political football in the regional cold war between Greece and Turkey, will end up being more divided than ever if the talks fail amid a buildup of arms on both sides.

"We are the victims of disputes between the two mainlands," lamented Anastasiades. "In London, we live together, in the United States we live together. But in Cyprus we cannot say hello to our compatriots."
On Friday last-minute diplomatic activity intensified, with Western and U.N. mediators piling pressure on Denktash to drop his opposition to a proposed framework accord.
Denktash, who wants sovereign equality, blames the Greek Cypriots for blocking a deal and accuses the EU of turning the talks into a "Greek tragedy."

"We have always said the Greek Cypriots are refusing to negotiate with us because they prefer the title of government of Cyprus rather than sharing powers with us," he told reporters. "Here, they saw our determination not to surrender to threats."
"It is a very big tragedy the EU has committed while the talks were going on in a positive atmosphere. It is a Greek tragedy," he said. "This is the last round until EU decides."
The two Cypriot communities have been estranged since 1963 when a government in which both took part collapsed amid violence, three years after independence from Britain.
The island has been divided since 1974 when Turkey occupied its north in response to a coup in the capital Nicosia engineered by the military junta then ruling Greece.

Denktash and Clerides, old sparring partners who have known and battled each other for nearly half a century since both were young, London-trained lawyers, have spent many many years of hard, fruitless bargaining with each other without a compromise.
